newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Tunisia to cut money market average rate by one point.
newsitem.headline: Tunisia to cut money market average rate by one point.

text.p: The key Tunisian average money market rate will be cut by one percentage point, Tunisian President Zine al-Abidine Ben Ali announced on Thursday.
The money market rate, which serves as a reference to bank interest rates, has been stable at 8.8125 percent since 1993.
President Ben Ali did not say when the new rate will come into force.
In the past, rate changes have taken effect immediately.
Ben Ali also announced that the premium for coverage of foreign exchange risks for development banks will be cut by two points with respect to credit for investment.

He said that the decision to cut the money market rate was taken "considering the progress that has been made in containing inflation, and in the aim of providing eased conditions for financing and credit so as to stimulate investment and revitalize Tunisian businesses."

"This will make it possible gradually to achieve the desired flexibility of interest rates, as an instrument for the stabilisation of the money market and a factor of economic vitality," Ben Ali added in a speech at the occasion of the 9th anniversary of his arrival to power.
Tunisia forecast an inflation rate of less than 4.5 percent this year after 6.2 percent in 1995.

Central Bank governor Mohamed Beji Hamda had earlier this year said in a report to Ben Ali that "efforts that should be made ... to contain inflation imply the interest rate playing a more active role in ensuring that the cost of money corresponds to its true price."

Development banks, generally joint ventures between the Tunisian state and Gulf states public funds, had maintained higher interest rates than domestic deposit banks because of long term loans rates they contracted before the fall of interest rates in the world's financial markets.
Tunisian investors had complained about these high rates which were between 14 and 15 percent and the measure announced by Ben Ali was aimed at reducing these rates, bankers said.
